target_year_over_year_context.explanation: The 2024 disclosures D145 and D250 establish the baseline policy: Significant Plans are measured quarterly, while All Other Plans are measured annually. The 2025 disclosures D153 and D154 reflect the same structural classification (Significant vs. All Other) but update the specific condition for quarterly measurement (now 'when certain conditions are met to trigger interim remeasurement' rather than automatic quarterly). D154 explicitly mirrors the annual measurement for All Other Plans. Although D265 notes an overall policy change to annual measurement for all plans unless triggered, D153/D154 describe the residual ongoing policy for the Significant Plans category which retains the quarterly trigger mechanism mentioned in D145/D250. The group captures the transition of the 'Significant Plan quarterly' and 'All Other Plan annual' topics.

materiality_analysis.reason: The 2025 disclosure changes the measurement frequency for 'Significant Plans' from automatic quarterly measurement to quarterly measurement 'when certain conditions are met to trigger interim remeasurement.' This introduces a conditionality that was not present in the previous 'quarterly, instead of annually' mandate, potentially allowing for less frequent remeasurement of significant obligations and assets depending on the trigger conditions. This is a meaningful change in the timing and certainty of financial reporting for pension obligations.
materiality_analysis.key_change: Introduction of conditional trigger for pension remeasurement

peer_results.rationale: BAC's candidate disclosures focus on summarizing the changes in fair value of plan assets and projected benefit obligations (bac_2024_8_D353) or the sensitivity of net periodic benefit cost to discount rates (bac_2024_8_D361). These do not compare directly to C's specific disclosure regarding the measurement frequency (quarterly vs. annual) and materiality threshold (90% of obligations) used to define its 'Significant Plans'. BAC's disclosures are related to pension accounting mechanics rather than the specific policy of distinguishing plans by measurement frequency based on obligation magnitude.

comparisons.peer_topic: Recognition of Funded Status of Pension and Postretirement Plans
comparisons.peer_summary: The firm recognizes the funded status of its defined benefit pension and postretirement plans in the consolidated balance sheets, recording $73 million in other assets and $344 million in other liabilities as of December 2024, compared to $93 million in other assets and $449 million in other liabilities as of December 2023.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and GS disclose the recognition of the funded status of their defined benefit pension and postretirement plans on the balance sheet. However, C provides specific quantitative thresholds for its disclosure policy, noting that its 'most significant' plans represent approximately 90% of global obligations and are measured quarterly, whereas GS discloses aggregate asset and liability amounts ($73 million and $344 million respectively) without defining a specific 'significant' threshold or measurement frequency in the same text. C focuses on the materiality of the plan set (90% of obligations) to justify quarterly measurement, while GS focuses on the resulting balance sheet line items.

sentences.text: The Significant Plans captured approximately 90% of the Company's global pension and postretirement benefit plan obligations as of December 31, 2024.
As of December 2024, other assets included $73 million (related to overfunded pension plans) and other liabilities included $344 million related to these plans.

comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm maintains funded and unfunded postretirement benefit plans providing medical and life insurance for eligible employees and retirees, which have no material impact on the Consolidated Financial Statements.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and JPM discuss the materiality and scope of their postretirement benefit plans. C explicitly states that its 'most significant' pension and postretirement plans cover approximately 90% of global obligations and are measured quarterly, implying materiality. In contrast, JPM states that its funded and unfunded postretirement benefit plans (providing medical and life insurance) have 'no material impact' on its Consolidated Financial Statements. This highlights a difference in the financial significance attributed to postretirement benefits between the two firms.

sentences.text: The Significant Plans captured approximately 90% of the Company's global pension and postretirement benefit plan obligations as of December 31, 2024.

comparisons.peer_summary: The table includes pension plans where the projected benefit obligation exceeded the fair value of plan assets, and the specific plans included may vary year-to-year based on their funding status as of December 31.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and MS address which pension plans are included in their significant disclosures based on their funding or obligation status. MS explicitly states that the pension plans included in its table of underfunded plans 'may differ based on their funding status as of December 31 of each year.' C similarly distinguishes between 'Significant Plans' (measured quarterly) and 'All Other Plans' (measured annually), where the 'Significant Plans' are defined by capturing approximately 90% of global obligations. Both use dynamic criteria (obligation share for C, funding status for MS) to determine the scope of their primary pension disclosures.

sentences.text: The plan obligations, plan assets and periodic plan expense for the Company's most significant pension and postretirement benefit plans (Significant Plans) are measured and disclosed quarterly, instead of annually.
All other plans (All Other Plans) are measured annually with a December 31 measurement date.
The pension plans included in the table above may differ based on their funding status as of December 31 of each year.
